Container With Most Water
Start with the widest container and always move the shorter wall inward. Moving the taller wall can never increase the area.
Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Array (in place)
Minimum Window Substring (contains all characters of t)
Trapping Rain Water
Two pointers, each tracking the max height seen from its side. Always process the side with the smaller max, because the water there is bounded by that max.
Longest Repeating Character Replacement (at most k changes)
A window is valid when length − count of its most frequent char ≤ k. maxFreq never needs to decrease: a smaller value can never produce a longer answer. O(n) time, O(26) space.
Find All Anagrams in a String / Permutation in String
A fixed window of size |p| with letter counts. Comparing two 26-length arrays is O(1), so the total is O(n). You can also keep a "matches" counter to avoid the array comparison.
Minimum Size Subarray Sum (sum ≥ target, positive numbers)

"Shortest valid window": expand right, then shrink left as long as the window stays valid. This only works because all values are positive. With negatives use prefix sums plus a monotonic deque. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Max Consecutive Ones III (flip at most k zeros)
"Longest valid window": the window is valid while it holds at most k zeros. Each index enters and leaves once, so O(n) time and O(1) space.
Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters (Fruit Into Baskets)
The map size is the number of distinct characters in the window. Trick: "exactly K distinct" = atMost(K) − atMost(K−1). O(n) time, O(k) space.
Squares of a Sorted Array (with negatives)
The largest square is always at one of the two ends, so two pointers moving inward fill the result from the back. O(n) instead of O(n log n) for square-then-sort.
Opposite-ends pointers vs same-direction (slow/fast) pointers vs sliding window

| Opposite ends | Slow / fast (same direction) | Sliding window
Start | L = 0, R = n - 1 | Both at 0 | Both at 0
Moves | Move the side that can improve the answer | Fast scans, slow marks the write position | R expands; L shrinks while the window is invalid
Needs | Sorted input or a symmetric property | In-place filtering | A condition that stays valid as the window shrinks
Examples | Two Sum II, Container With Most Water, 3Sum | Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes | Longest Substring Without Repeating, Min Window
Time | O(n) | O(n) | O(n)
Rule of thumb: sorted array and a pair question → opposite ends. Rewrite the array in place → slow/fast. "Longest/shortest contiguous part that satisfies X" → sliding window.
Fixed-size window vs variable-size window

| Fixed size k | Variable size
Question wording | "every window of size k" | "longest / shortest subarray such that…"
L moves | Exactly when R ≥ k (L = R - k + 1) | In a while loop until the window is valid again
Answer updated | Once per R after the first k | After shrinking (longest) or while shrinking (shortest)
Examples | Max sum of size K, Find All Anagrams | Minimum Size Subarray Sum, Fruit Into Baskets
Interview tip: for "shortest" windows, update the answer inside the while loop (before removing); for "longest", update after it.
Window state: int[128] vs HashMap vs last-seen index map

| int[128] counts | HashMap counts | Last-seen index
Character set | ASCII | Any | Any (array if ASCII)
How L moves | One step at a time in a while loop | One step at a time | Jumps: L = max(L, last[c] + 1)
Speed | Fastest | Slower (boxing, hashing) | Fast, fewer steps
Good for | Anagram / permutation windows | Distinct-count windows with "map.size()" | No-repeat substring
Rule of thumb: use an array when the alphabet is small. Use a HashMap when you need the number of distinct keys (remove the key when its count hits 0, so size() stays correct).
"At most K" vs "exactly K": why exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1)

| At most K | Exactly K
Window monotonic? | Yes: shrinking keeps it valid | No: shrinking can drop below K
Direct sliding window | Works | Does not work cleanly
Counting trick | Each R adds R - L + 1 subarrays | atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1)
Example | Subarrays with at most K distinct | Subarrays with exactly K distinct, Binary Subarrays With Sum
Interview tip: when "exactly" breaks the window, reach for this subtraction. It is a common follow-up.
